data.title: TX - 2024 - Form L Audited Financial Statements
data.highlights: Applicants are required to provide their most recent audited financial statements as part of the RFA application process. This ensures financial due diligence for the demonstration project focused on rural populations with intellectual or developmental disabilities.

data.title: TX - 2024 - FORM H: Internal Controls Questionnaire
data.highlights: This document outlines required internal controls and financial procedures for applicants to the HHSC Houston Preventative and Primary Health Services grant. It emphasizes the necessity for proper accounting systems, segregation of direct and indirect costs, written policies, and robust procedures that ensure compliance with federal and state grant requirements. Applicants must demonstrate capability to maintain accurate records and facilitate audits.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Form K: Indirect Cost Rate Agreement
data.highlights: This document provides guidance for applicants submitting indirect cost rate agreements as part of the proposal process for the IDD Multi-Assistance Center Demonstration Project in Texas. Respondents are instructed to include a copy of their most recently approved indirect cost rate agreement.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Form F, Subcontracting Information
data.highlights: This document is a required form for applicants responding to the Houston Preventative and Primary Health Services RFA. It collects detailed information about planned subcontractors who will provide direct services. No awards or recipients are named at this stage.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Attachment K-1, One Time Start-up Costs
data.highlights: This guidance outlines allowable start-up costs for organizations applying under Texas' Rural Mental Health Initiative Grant Program. It emphasizes the need for expenditures to be reasonable, necessary, and directly related to project launch, and provides examples of typically permissible and impermissible costs. HHSC will approve start-up costs through grantee budget submissions following federal and state grant management standards.

data.title: TX - 2025 - Form E: Performance Measures and Funding Ceiling Request
data.highlights: This form from Texas HHSC is used to capture proposed funding requests, anticipated number of clients to be served, and requested budgets across core service categories. Applicants must define their program impact via unduplicated clients and propose a funding ceiling for negotiations.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Form D Zip Codes Served (AlphaNum)
data.highlights: This document outlines eligible zip codes for applicants to select service areas for the Houston Preventative and Primary Health Services RFA. Applicants are instructed to focus on at-risk and distressed areas to target health disparities and underserved populations. It supports intervention in rural and vulnerable zones within Houston and Harris County.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Form F, Therapy Services
data.highlights: This form collects the applicant's comprehensive plan to provide a range of therapy and referral services at the Multi-Assistance Center demonstration project for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities. It requires estimates for annual unique beneficiaries and asks for both quantitative and qualitative outcome measures.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Form C Work Plan
data.highlights: This supporting work plan form is part of the PPHS RFA application package. Applicants must detail the unique needs in their proposed service area and how their services will improve access to preventative and primary care for low-income, uninsured, or Medicaid-covered Texans. The form reinforces accountability by requiring a certification of accuracy from an authorized representative.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Form E Medical Services
data.highlights: The MAC demonstration project aims to deliver comprehensive, on-site medical and dental services for individuals with intellectual or developmental disabilities, enhancing convenience and access to care. Applicants are required to describe how these services will be routinely available and estimate annual service volumes. Qualitative and quantifiable outcomes are expected to gauge the project's effectiveness.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Attachment F-1, Letters of Support
data.highlights: Attachment F-1 provides instructions for applicants to furnish a letter of support from local mental or behavioral health authorities operating in the proposed project's rural service area. It references compliance with specific RFA sections for eligibility and proposal requirements.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Form B-2, Non-Profit or For-Profit Entity
data.highlights: This document serves as a supporting form for the Houston Preventative and Primary Health Services RFA, requiring applicants to list their board members, officers, key personnel, and relevant contact details. It is designed to verify organizational structure and personnel for submitting entities.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Form C, Narrative Proposal
data.highlights: This application form is for responding organizations proposing to operate a Multi-Assistance Center (MAC) that delivers coordinated medical, therapy, and non-medical services for individuals with IDD and other related conditions in Texas. The form focuses on respondents' plans for service delivery, counties served, and organizational structure. Emphasis is on single-point-of-contact coordinators who help families navigate access to services and community partnerships.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Form B, Administrative Entity Information
data.highlights: Form B is an administrative application attachment that collects information about the respondent business entity, including ownership structure, company profile, workforce, and intended subcontractors. It ensures that applicants for the Houston Preventative and Primary Health Services RHTP-funded initiative are organizationally qualified and transparent regarding their structure and capability. No funding or awards are detailed in this document.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Attachment C-2, Audited Financial Reports
data.highlights: This supporting document provides instructions for applicants to submit their most recently audited financial report as part of the Rural Mental Health Initiative Grant Program application. It is intended to ensure financial transparency and compliance for organizations seeking funding under the RHTP-related opportunity.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Form A, Face Page
data.highlights: Form A Face Page collects core applicant and proposed project data as part of the RFA for the Multi-Assistance Center Demonstration Project targeting people with intellectual or developmental disabilities. It instructs applicants to provide organizational information, funding request details, covered counties, and key contacts as a required part of the application submission.

data.title: TX - 2023 - Exhibit H, Evaluation Tool RFA No. HHS0014610
data.highlights: This exhibit defines the evaluation criteria for scoring applications submitted under the Texas Multi-Assistance Center Demonstration Project RFA (HHS0014610) for IDD populations. Five main criteria are weighted, focusing on single-point coordination, medical services, therapy services, non-medical services, and budget proposal quality. Evaluation tools are designed to promote holistic, integrated service delivery in rural settings.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Exhibit E, Evaluation Tool
data.highlights: This document provides guidance for evaluating applications submitted under the Houston Preventative and Primary Health Services RFA. Scoring is based primarily on how well applicants demonstrate local unmet need, supported by quantitative data and linkage to distress ratings. Each application criterion must be evaluated by at least 3 reviewers, ensuring an objective review process.

data.title: TX - 2024 - Exhibit D, Key Personnel
data.highlights: This document is a required supporting form for applicants to identify and provide contact details for the key personnel involved in managing the Multi-Assistance Center Demonstration Project for Intellectual or Developmental Disabilities (IDD). It is used as part of the application package for the Texas RHTP RFA HHS0014610. The file collects project contacts, executive leadership, and up to four key project stakeholders.

data.title: TX - 2019 - RFA No. HHS0014532 Exhibit D Data Use Agreement Between The Texas Health And Human Services System And Contractor
data.highlights: This Data Use Agreement governs the handling, security, and privacy of Confidential Information by contractors and subcontractors participating in the Houston Preventative and Primary Health Services (PPHS) RFA. It establishes the safeguards required for protected health information and describes breach notification, mitigation, and correction procedures. The DUA sets requirements for compliance with HIPAA, Texas regulations, and federal standards. Key contacts: Chief Privacy Officer privacy@hhsc.state.tx.us

data.highlights: This is a Data Use Agreement (DUA) required for the Texas HHSC IDD Multi-Assistance Center Demonstration Project RFA applicants and subawardees, detailing responsibilities, breach notification, and protections for confidential information in compliance with HIPAA, state, and federal law. It sets forth procedures for handling Protected Health Information (PHI), breach response, subcontractor obligations, and HHS rights. The DUA underscores the importance of security, privacy, and regulatory adherence for all program data transactions under this RHTP-funded Medicaid rural demonstration.

ARTICLE 1. PURPOSE; APPLICABILITY; ORDER OF PRECEDENCE The purpose of this DUA is to facilitate access to, creation, receipt, maintenance, use, disclosure or transmission of Confidential Information with Contractor, and describe Contractor’s rights and obligations with respect to the Confidential Information and the limited purposes for which the Contractor may create, receive, maintain, use, disclose or have access to Confidential Information. This DUA also describes HHS’s remedies in the event of Contractor’s noncompliance with its obligations under this DUA. This DUA applies to both HHS business associates, as “business associate” is defined in the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), and contractors who are not business associates, who create, receive, maintain, use, disclose or have access to Confidential Information on behalf of HHS, its programs or clients as described in the Base Contract. As a best practice, HHS requires its contractors to comply with the terms of this DUA to safeguard all types of Confidential Information. As of the Effective Date of this DUA, if any provision of the Base Contract conflicts with this DUA, this DUA controls. ARTICLE 2. DEFINITIONS For the purposes of this DUA, capitalized, underlined terms have the following meanings: “Authorized Purpose” means the specific purpose or purposes described in the Base Contract for Contractor to fulfill its obligations under the Base Contract, or any other purpose expressly authorized by HHS in writing in advance. “Authorized User” means a person: (1) Who is authorized to create, receive, maintain, have access to, process, view, handle, examine, interpret, or analyze Confidential Information pursuant to this DUA; (2) For whom Contractor warrants and represents has a demonstrable need to create, receive, maintain, use, disclose or have access to the Confidential Information; and (3) Who has agreed in writing to be bound by the disclosure and use limitations pertaining to the Confidential Information as required by this DUA. “Breach” means an impermissible use or disclosure of electronic or non-electronic sensitive personal information by an unauthorized person or for an unauthorized purpose that compromises the security or privacy of Confidential Information such that the use or disclosure poses a risk of reputational harm, theft of financial information, identity theft, or medical identity theft. Any acquisition, access, use, disclosure or loss of Confidential Information other than as permitted by this HHS Data Use Agreement v.8.5 , 2019 1 of 11

DUA shall be presumed to be a Breach unless Contractor demonstrates, based on a risk assessment, that there is a low probability that the Confidential Information has been compromised. “Confidential Information” means any communication or record (whether oral, written, electronically stored or transmitted, or in any other form) provided to or made available to Contractor or that Contractor may create, receive, maintain, use, disclose or have access to on behalf of HHS that consists of or includes any or all of the following: (1) Education records as defined in the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, 20 U.S.C. §1232g; 34 C.F.R. Part 99 (2) Federal Tax Information as defined in Internal Revenue Code §6103 and Internal Revenue Service Publication 1075; (3) Personal Identifying Information (PII) as defined in Texas Business and Commerce Code, Chapter 521; (4) Protected Health Information (PHI) in any form including without limitation, Electronic Protected Health Information or Unsecured Protected Health Information as defined in 45 C.F.R. §160.103; (5) Sensitive Personal Information (SPI) as defined in Texas Business and Commerce Code, Chapter 521; (6) Social Security Administration Data, including, without limitation, Medicaid information means disclosures of information made by the Social Security Administration or the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services from a federal system of records for administration of federally funded benefit programs under the Social Security Act, 42 U.S.C., Chapter 7; (7) All privileged work product; (8) All information designated as confidential under the constitution and laws of the State of Texas and of the United States, including the Texas Health & Safety Code and the Texas Public Information Act, Texas Government Code, Chapter 552. “Destroy”, “Destruction”, for Confidential Information, means: (1) Paper, film, or other hard copy media have been shredded or destroyed such that the Confidential Information cannot be read or otherwise cannot be reconstructed. Redaction is specifically excluded as a means of data destruction. (2) Electronic media have been cleared, purged, or destroyed consistent with NIST Special Publication 800-88, " Guidelines for Media Sanitization , " such that the Confidential Information cannot be retrieved. “Discover, Discovery” means the first day on which a Breach becomes known to Contractor, or, by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known to Contractor. “Legally Authorized Representative” of an individual, including as provided in 45 CFR 435.923 (authorized representative); 45 CFR 164.502(g)(1) (personal representative); Tex. Occ. Code § 151.002(6); Tex. H. & S. Code §166.164 (medical power of attorney); and Texas Estates Code § 22.031 (representative). “Required by Law” means a mandate contained in law that compels an entity to use or disclose Confidential Information that is enforceable in a court of law, including court orders, warrants, subpoenas or investigative demands. data.title: AZ - 2025 - Federal Funding Requirements for RHTP
data.highlights: This document outlines federal programmatic, privacy, security, and fiscal requirements for recipients of RHTP funding. It details both required grant assurances and explicit funding prohibitions, including cost allocation, prohibition on lobbying, research, construction, and specific limits on clinical payments. Additional cybersecurity, program income, and publication acknowledgment requirements are also described.

Funding is subject to all restrictions and requirements described in the example initiative. ● Funds may not be used for clinician salaries. data.title: LA - 2026 - Rural Collaborative Provider Models Program Answers to Submitted Questions July 23, 2026
data.highlights: This document answers applicant questions regarding eligible uses of RHTP funds, allowable applicant types, allowable partnerships, and project structuring for the Louisiana Rural Collaborative Provider Models Program Year 1 NOFO. It clarifies that funding cannot replace reimbursable clinical payments, but supports network development, workforce deployment, and service expansion. Only qualified, LDH-licensed rural health providers are eligible to apply as leads; partners may include academic institutions and other organizations.

keyDates.label: Rural Collaborative Provider Models Program Answers to Submitted Questions , 2026 These questions and answers are for the Louisiana Rural Collaborative Provider Models Program, Year 1 Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO). Submitted questions were combined and modified in the interest of brevity. This document is intended to be a resource for all prospective applicants. Application/General Program Questions 1. Does having multiple rural sites in a consortium application require a single lead applicant/fiscal agent, or can costs be split across separate applications tied to one shared Statement of Work? Proposals involving a consortium of organizations should have a lead applicant designated. If awarded that lead applicant organization will executed a Cooperative Endeavor Agreement (CEA) with LDH. The CEA will allow for sub-agreements with partners, if warranted and justified. 2. For a shared regional dental care coordinator position serving multiple rural FQHCs and LSU Health School of Dentistry jointly, how should the applicant structure funding, employment, and reporting lines — for example, should one FQHC serve as the sole employer of record with the position's time/cost allocated across partner sites via an MOU, or does LDH allow the position to be jointly funded and supervised across multiple applicant/partner organizations directly? Proposals involving a consortium of organizations should have a lead applicant designated. If awarded that lead applicant organization will executed a Cooperative Endeavor Agreement (CEA) with LDH. The lead applicant or a partner may serve as sole employer of record and be eligible for reimbursement. Eligible Use of Funds 1. Does this funding allow for direct payments to a specialist provider, provider group, or hospital employer for offering services in a rural area? Eg - Rural Hospital A offers funding from the grant to Provider Group B for the provision of services at A. No. Per CMS guidance, RHTP funds cannot be used to replace payment for clinical services that could be reimbursed by insurance. Further RHTP funds cannot duplicate billable services and/or attempt to change payment amounts of existing fee schedules. Examples of acceptable use of funds are in the table below. Category Examples Network Development Partnership formation, governance, legal agreements, shared operating models Workforce Deployment Provider rotation programs, travel support, onboarding, scheduling systems Service Expansion Startup costs for shared specialty, behavioral health, dental, pharmacy, and care coordination services

Rural Collaborative Provider Models Program Answers to Submitted Questions , 2026 Administrative Infrastructure Referral management, provider scheduling, regional coordination Operational Transition Workflow redesign, implementation support, launch costs Performance Monitoring Access, utilization, service availability, and quality reporting 2. May this funding be used to make payments from specialists outside a rural area to retain their existing services in that rural area? Eg- Urban Provider Group A currently provides services to Rural Hospital B. Rural Hospital B uses funding from the grant to pay A additional money in order to retain their services at B. No. Per CMS guidance, RHTP funds cannot be used to replace payment for clinical services that could be reimbursed by insurance. Further RHTP funds cannot duplicate billable services and/or attempt to change payment amounts of existing fee schedules. 3. In regards to the priority variable "shared dental services", can the rural provider (e.g, FQHC) use funds for lodging/housing of dental students/post-doctoral dental residents on a multi-week rural rotation or is funding limited to mileage/per diem only? If lodging/housing is not allowable, may it be counted toward the applicant's 10% in-kind match if provided by a partner organization, for example an AHEC? Is there a per diem cap for use with rotation student/resident travel stipends? Yes, lodging can be requested as travel support. All requested travel support must be in compliance with Federal Travel Regulations (FTR), codified in 41 CFR Chapters 300-304. 4. In the process of developing networks, coordinating care, etc., is it permissible to use these funds to pay staff wages and salaries for performing these duties? Are there restrictions on paying a portion of a shared coordinator's salary to an entity where that person is jointly employed or supervised by both the rural applicant and the academic partner? Can a pediatric speech therapy clinic use the funds to hire a Coordinator for the development of partnerships? Requests for salaries/wages in support of establishing, developing, coordinating or maintaining a collaborative provider program must be detailed and justified in the application for LDH consideration. Federal funds must be used to supplement (add to), enhance, or expand existing services for program activities and not replace those funds that have been appropriated for the same purpose. A subrecipient may not use Federal grant funds to defray any costs that the recipient is already obligated to pay. The possibility of supplanting will be the subject of careful application review, possible pre-award review, post-award monitoring, and audit of any finding.

Rural Collaborative Provider Models Program Answers to Submitted Questions , 2026 Eligible Organizations/Programs 1. Does the program consider workforce infrastructure organizations that directly support licensed rural providers eligible to apply under the "Other" organization type? If not, would a formal partnership or subrecipient arrangement with a licensed rural provider satisfy the eligibility requirement? Applicants must qualify as “rural” under the Louisiana Rural Health Transformation Program definition and methodology AND be licensed by LDH or applicable licensing agency as a: o Rural Health Clinic (RHCs) o Federally Qualified Health Center (FQHCs) or look-alikes o Critical Access Hospital (CAHs) o Rural Hospital o Rural EMS provider o Rural behavioral health or substance use provider o Independent rural practice (Rural physician or physician group, pharmacy, dentist) 3. Would a Pediatric Speech therapy clinic, serving rural patients, be eligible for this grant? Yes. Applicants must qualify as “rural” under the Louisiana Rural Health Transformation Program definition and methodology AND be licensed by LDH or applicable licensing agency. 4. Can an academic institution (e.g., a dental school) be named as a formal partner/subcontractor in the Statement of Work even though it is not itself eligible to apply Yes, an academic institution can serve as a partner/subcontractor in collaborative provider applications.

data.title: KS - 2026 - Centralized Verification Organization RFP Questions and Answers
data.highlights: This document provides answers to vendor questions regarding the RHTP-funded Centralized Verification Organization RFP for Kansas. The pilot will begin with phased onboarding of Medicaid managed care organizations, a commercial payer, and a limited hospital sample. The project aims to establish a statewide, scalable, technology-agnostic credentialing infrastructure with centralized verification to improve quality, efficiency, and compliance across Kansas healthcare organizations. Key contacts: CCO Specialist (Healthworks)

keyDates.label: Centralized Verification Organization RFP Questions and Answers Question: Assuming a tiered approach, how many practitioners are expected to be processed in the first year? All 17,000 practitioners? Number requiring initial credentialing Response Healthworks is seeking the expertise of the selected Centralized Verification Organization (CVO) to recommend a phased implementation strategy for the pilot period from September 2026 through , 2027. The intent of the pilot is not to immediately onboard all approximately 17,000 practitioners. Rather, respondents should propose an implementation approach that supports a successful, scalable rollout while balancing operational readiness, stakeholder participation, and program objectives. Number requiring recredentialing if picking up participating practitioners at recredentialing time Response Kansas statutes and regulations do not prescribe a specific recredentialing cycle. Most Kansas hospitals recredential practitioners every two years to align with medical staff bylaws and Joint Commission standards. Kansas Medicaid Managed Care Organizations generally follow NCQA standards, which require recredentialing at least every 36 months. One objective of the CCV Pilot is to facilitate collaboration among participating organizations to identify opportunities for greater standardization of credentialing processes, including recredentialing timelines, where appropriate. Number participating during the pilot year Response Healthworks is relying on the selected CVO's experience implementing centralized credentialing programs to recommend an appropriate provider and payer ramp-up strategy. Annual improvement goals have been established under the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP); however, no specific provider participation targets have been established for each year of the pilot. The selected CVO will assist Healthworks and participating stakeholders in developing policies, procedures, and implementation strategies that support measured and sustainable growth. Recredentialing timeline consolidation across participating organizations Response
keyDates.location: Question: Verification Scope There is reference to hospitals, but verification scope is NCQA. Is the expectation that processing be performed in compliance with NCQA only? Response No. The selected CVO is expected to perform primary source verification activities in accordance with applicable NCQA standards while recognizing that participating hospitals, health plans, and other participating organizations remain subject to their own accreditation standards, regulatory requirements, Conditions of Participation, and organizational credentialing policies. One objective of the pilot is to identify opportunities to standardize credentialing policies and verification processes where appropriate while allowing participating organizations to maintain any additional requirements necessary to satisfy their respective regulatory and accreditation obligations. Question: Offshore / Onshore Do you require PSV services to be conducted exclusively onshore? Response The RFP does not expressly prohibit offshore services. However, respondents should recognize that Healthworks places significant value on data security, HIPAA compliance, operational transparency, responsiveness, and stakeholder confidence. While there is no general federal prohibition on offshore primary source verification activities, Healthworks recognizes that many healthcare organizations prefer or require onshore operations because they: • Enhance confidence in HIPAA compliance and data security. • Simplify oversight and auditing. • Reduce concerns regarding foreign access to credentialing information. • Align with the expectations of hospitals, payers, regulators, and participating organizations. • Improve responsiveness during audits, surveys, and implementation activities.

A primary objective of the pilot is to evaluate opportunities for standardization while respecting each participating organization's regulatory, accreditation, and operational requirements. The selected CVO is expected to assist in developing recommendations regarding standardized credentialing policies and recredentialing practices. Healthworks currently anticipates beginning implementation with one participating payer and one small hospital to validate workflows, governance processes, and technology integration before expanding to additional participating organizations. data.title: PA - 2026 - FQHC & FQHC Look-Alikes – Modernizing Healthcare Technology and Interoperability Frequently Asked Questions
data.highlights: This FAQ outlines eligibility and allowable use of funds for the Pennsylvania RHTP-funded opportunity supporting FQHCs and FQHC Look-Alikes in eligible rural counties to purchase and implement CEHRT systems and connect to the state HIE (P3N). Program payments are available up to $300,000 per entity. The guidance specifies program rules, eligible applicants, geographic requirements, and allowable costs such as CEHRT acquisition and onboarding to P3N via certified HIOs.

keyDates.label: FQHC & FQHC Look-Alikes – Modernizing Healthcare Technology and Interoperability Frequently Asked Questions Updated: 7/22/2026 These FAQs apply only to the FQHC & FQHC Look-Alikes – Modernizing Healthcare Technology and Interoperability program payment. 1. What are the eligibility requirements for qualified entities? Entities must complete all eligibility certification sections in full either by submitting the online form or by filling out the form and submitting it via email. Prior to submission, entities should verify that they have accurately completed all the sections of the eligibility certification and have emailed all documents requested in those sections. If any portion of the eligibility certification is incomplete, the entity will not be eligible for payment. If any attachment is not included or is incomplete, the entity will not be eligible for payment. For this program payment, a “qualified entity” is a Medicaid-enrolled provider that is an FQHC or FQHC look-alike that meet Federal qualifications under Section 330 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. § 254b). The entity must certify that: • The entity meets Federal qualifications under Section 330 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. § 254b). • The entity is an enrolled provider in Pennsylvania’s Medical Assistance Program. • The entity currently operates in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. Current operation means that the entity provides health care services, has at least one physical location in Pennsylvania, and has been in operation since at least , 2025. • The entity will be in full operation in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania on the date funding is received and is not at risk of closure. • The entity operates in one or more of the Pennsylvania RHTP regions. • The entity is located in RHTP-eligible rural counties classes 2A-8. • The entity provides services to residents of RHTP-eligible rural counties classes 4-8 or in a HRSA rural health area in RHTP-eligible rural counties classes 2A and 3. • The entity shall use the funding for the qualified activities. 1

This funding can be used for purchasing and implementing a CEHRT system in accordance with 45 CFR § 170.315; and becoming a participant in one of the Commonwealth’s five certified HIOs and fully onboarding to the statewide HIE, the P3N. 12. If an FQHC or FQHC look-alike has a CEHRT, but is not connected directly to one of the 5 HIOS are they eligible for funding and reimbursement? Yes. Funding can be used solely for becoming a participant in one of the Commonwealth’s five certified HIOs and fully onboarding to the statewide HIE, the P3N. 13. Can an FQHC or FQHC look-alike use this funding to pay a third-party consultant to guide the transition and implementation of the CEHRT system and P3N HIO onboarding? Yes, payment to a third-party consultant to guide the transition and implementation of the CEHRT system and P3N HIO onboarding is an allowable cost. 14. What are the Commonwealth’s five certified HIOs? A list of the five P3N certified HIOs is available here: 2025-05-06-choose-your-hio.pdf 15. What constitutes becoming a participant in one of the Commonwealth’s five certified HIOs and fully onboarding to the statewide HIE, the P3N? Becoming a participant in one of the Commonwealth’s five certified HIOs and fully onboarding to the statewide health information exchange (HIE), the Pennsylvania Patient and Provider Network (“P3N”) means that the entity’s EHR has functionality to share HL7 Admission, Discharge, and Transfer message documents (ADTs) and discharge summary/continuity of care documents (CCDs) as well as have the ability to query and retrieve Historical Lists (medications, allergies, etc.) and Longitudinal Medical Records. The standards for the document types listed above must meet CMS Meaningful Use standards which currently follow the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) - July 2022 - Version 3. 16. Can a connection to a National E-Health Exchange satisfy the activity requirement to become a participant in one of the Commonwealth’s five certified HIOs? No. 5

data.title: UT - 2026 - Utah RHTP SHIFT 3.2 Rural Health Provider Networks RFGA
data.highlights:
This RFGA will fund up to six rural health provider networks in Utah to expand, strengthen, and connect clinical service providers through shared operational and care models. Eligible applicants must be Utah-based and demonstrate formal collaboration among at least three different rural healthcare facilities. Program priorities include forming sustainable networks to expand access, streamline administration, integrate behavioral, maternal, oral, and trauma health, and set up performance evaluation and data tracking to drive long-term transformation. keyDates.label: 17. Drug-Free Workplace Certification. As required by Executive Order No. 90-5 dated , 1990, issued by the Governor of Indiana, the Contractor hereby covenants and agrees to make a good faith effort to provide and maintain a drug-free workplace. The Contractor will give written notice to the State within ten (10) days after receiving actual notice that the Contractor, or an employee of the Contractor in the State of Indiana, has been convicted of a criminal drug violation occurring in the workplace. In the event the State determines that any independent verification and validation ("IV&V") oversight is required by the State during the term of this Contract, the Contractor shall comply with any such oversight during the term of this Contract, pursuant to which an independent third-party review may be conducted by a reviewer selected by the State, for the purpose of verifying that the Contractor has performed its obligations in compliance with the terms of this Contract. data.title: TN - 2025 - overview
data.highlights:
The Rural Health Transformation (RHT) Program is a $50 billion initiative spanning FY2026–2030 to support system-wide change in rural health delivery nationwide. States compete for federal cooperative agreements to improve health care access, quality, sustainability, and capacity through technology innovation, workforce recruitment, and new payment and care models. data.title: LA - 2026 - Rural Medicaid APM Program Answers to Submitted Questions July 19, 2026
data.highlights: This document provides detailed answers to applicant questions for the Louisiana Medicaid RHTP Year 1 NOFO, covering eligible uses of funding, cost-share requirements, performance payment structure, and rural eligibility criteria. It clarifies distinctions between infrastructure, capacity-building, and performance-based activities, and offers guidance on allowable costs, measurement, and application scoring. The guidance emphasizes non-duplication of funding, accountability for quality and cost improvement, and the focus on Medicaid rural populations.

keyDates.label: Rural Medicaid APM Program Answers to Submitted Questions , 2026 These questions and answers are for the Louisiana Rural Medicaid Alternative Payment Models Program, Year 1 Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO). Submitted questions were combined and modified in the interest of brevity. This document is intended to be a resource for all prospective applicants. Application/General Program Questions 1. Can organizations apply under Lane 2 (model still evolving into rural areas), and also apply for infrastructure/capacity-building support to scale/tailor the model AND for funding to support new activities? Lane 2 can request infrastructure funding to scale/tailor the model to rural areas. Lane 2 applicants may also propose 'new activities' as additional uses if justified in the context of advancing LDH's target care model. Approval of such additional uses is at the sole discretion of LDH. 2. What parameters need to be fulfilled for implementing VBC? Applicant should refer to Section A for a description of LDH's target care model and Appendix C for a description of provider capabilities that are typically needed to successfully implement value-based care models. 3. May Lane 1 applicants propose one integrated care-coordination program addressing multiple chronic conditions (e.g., diabetes, hypertension, obesity, behavioral health, COPD/asthma), or does LDH recommend focusing on a single disease area? Yes, one integrated program covering multiple chronic conditions is consistent with the target model. LDH does not require a single-disease focus. 4. What is the scope and timeline for the Data Analytics Platform LDH may provide in Year 2? Will LDH consider funding an advanced analytics & population-health platform in Year 1 and ongoing? The state is currently exploring options for shared data and analytics solutions for future grant years. Such access is not guaranteed as part of this NOFO. This NOFO is for a single grant year. Awards in this year are not a guarantee of future funding Eligible Use of Funds 1. Can a Rural Hospital Value Incentive Program (RHVIP) be funded through transformation funds? The RHVIP would use a financial model like the Managed Care Incentive Payment (MCIP) program; measures aligned with RHTP and awarded only when outcomes are met; rural - relevant measures (screenings, reducing ED visits,

Rural Medicaid APM Program Answers to Submitted Questions , 2026 chronic disease management); the State would support the VBC strategy with transformation funds that then receive a federal match. Applicants in Lane 1 (paid to get ready) may may p ropose projects that receive funding for annual preformance payments for achieving quality metrics. These metrics should be selected from the list in Appendix B, with proposed baseline and target figures to be aligned on with LDH. However, note that all applicants are required to describe how their proposed interventions are aligned to LDH's target care model, as described in the NOFO. Applications will be scored in part on how materially they advance an applicant toward the target model. Additionally, applicants must describe how RHTP funds are not duplicative with existing sources of funding, including the Managed Care Incentive Payment (MCIP) program. RHTP cannot pay again for the same activity, measure, or population/period those programs already cov er. LDH will not provide guidance on whether any RHTP funds are eligible for a federal match. Applicant is responsible for verifying that any such use of funds complies with all applicable laws and regulations. RHTP funds may not be used to support any activity, service, or expenditure for which federal matching funds are claimed or received. Applicants proposing pilots intended to transition to federally matched programs (such as Medicaid state plan or waiver services) must demonstrate t hat RHTP funding will end before any federal match is drawn. Applicants are responsible for ensuring compliance with all applicable federal laws and regulations, including prohibitions on using federal funds as the state or nonfederal share of another fede ral program. 2. As an RHC, if we apply and get funds approved, does it change our PPS rate, or is this in addition to the PPS rate? Applicants must describe how RHTP funds are not duplicative with existing sources of funding. RHTP cannot pay again for the s ame activity, measure, or population/period those programs already cover. Applicants should inquire directly with other programs whether accepting RHTP funds may impact their eligibility for or terms of participation in other programs. 3. Can funds be used t o develop informational materials such as a website and marketing materials to explain the APM/VBC construct from patient, provider, and payer perspectives? Development of informational materials could qualify as a form of technical assistance if the materials are provider and / or patient - facing, tied to a specific population and

Rural Medicaid APM Program Answers to Submitted Questions , 2026 model, and meet other criteria as described in the NOFO. Expenses related to pro duction of promotional items are not reimbursable. 4. Can funds be used to hire consultants to help define workflows, contract terms, infrastructure, training/education, or change management related to implementing a VBC APM? Yes. Consultants for workflow redesign, training, and change management may qualify as allowable technical assistance. 5. Can funds be used to staff a quality manager? Would this be subject to the ~6 months referenced in Section D3? Yes, staffing a quality manager may be an allowable use if tied to a defined population, intervention, role, timeline, and reporting requirement. Funding for operational (i.e., ongoing) staff or FTE support under this funding opportunity may not exceed 6 months. 6. Rural hospital(s) plan an evidence-based clinical care model with a clinical registry and analytics platform (patient identification, outcomes tracking, care coordination, QI, population health, quality reporting, APM participation, and dissemination of protocols). Is this an allowable transformation activity? May funds support personnel (registry coordinators, clinical data abstractors, data analysts) to develop/operate the registry and analytics platform? Yes. A registry/analytics build tied to a defined population, interventions, and outcomes is allowable. Staff to build and run it (coordinators, abstractors, analysts) are fundable when tied to the defined work. Funding for all operational (i.e., ongoing) staff or FTE support may not exceed 6 months. 7. Can a portion of the staffing funds be for existing staff whose time will be allocated to implementing this program? Yes. Existing staff time can be requested if it is tied to a defined role/population, documented, and not already paid by another source. 8. Section D3 allows 'interim data solutions for Year 1 implementation,' while D4 prohibits 'standalone platform purchases.' If we contract for analytics/registry/care- gap tools tied to a defined population and intervention, is a time-limited (e.g., 12- month) license/subscription plus implementation services allowable? Where does LDH draw the line? Time-limited funding for analytical tools that are tied to a defined population and intervention is an acceptable uses of funds. "Standalone platform purchases" refers to

Rural Medicaid APM Program Answers to Submitted Questions , 2026 purchases of analytical tools / capabilities that lack a clear connection to the proposed project and /or an accompanying plan to update related workflows and operations to ensure insights from the tool are actively used to improve quality and total cost of care. Example: the tool provides revenue capture analytics as well as VBC insights. Only VBC insights portion of the platform can be funded through this funding opportunity Time-limited licenses or subscriptions for analytics, registry, or care-gap tools are allowable when the tool is tied to a defined population and intervention and the applicant has a plan to integrate the tool's outputs into workflows and operations. Implementation services for such tools are also allowable. "Standalone platform purchases" refers to acquisitions of analytical tools or capabilities that lack a clear connection to the proposed intervention, or that have no accompanying plan for how insights will be used to improve quality and total cost of care. The distinction is not the purchase structure (license vs. subscription) but whether the tool is operationally connected to the funded project. Where a platform bundles allowable and non- allowable functions, only the portion supporting the funded intervention may be charged to this funding opportunity. Example: a platform that provides both revenue capture analytics and VBC insights. Only the VBC insights portion is eligible; the revenue capture portion must be funded through other means and costs must be allocated accordingly. 9. Can funds be used to pay for legal work related to development, contracting, and compliance for our VBC/APM, including modifications needed for rural implementation? Legal work for contracting/compliance may qualify as technical assistance or an 'additional use of funds' if reasonable, tied to implementation, and not fundable through other means. LDH will review and approve such uses of funds at its sole discretion. 10. Section D3 suggests care coordination and ILOS services may be paid if unreimbursed and tied to a defined population. Please elaborate on the requirements. Would staffing to support ILOS-compliant services also be subject to the Staff/FTE ~6-month constraint? Yes - care coordination and ILOS-type activities are fundable if unreimbursed, tied to a defined population, and documented. Applicants must describe how RHTP funds are not duplicative with existing sources of funding (e.g., ILOS services for a particular member cannot already be funded through their MCO). RHTP cannot pay again for the same activity, measure, or population/period those programs already cover.

Rural Medicaid APM Program Answers to Submitted Questions , 2026 The constraint on staffing applies to direct requests to fund specific roles and positions (i.e., guaranteed funding for a particular role). If, however, an applicant requests support from LDH for new ILOS services, the applicant can hire staff and pay them with funds received for those services. Because funding is based on the services and not specific staff, this would not trigger the 6-month constraint. The 6-month constraint is designed to encourage applicants to consider sustainable sources of funding that may exist beyond the scope of the Rural Health Transformation Program. In the above scenario for example, new ILOS services, once established, could potentially become reimbursable through Medicaid MCOs or fee-for-service. 11. The NOFO discusses PMPY payments; we assume those are annual payments for retrospective services. Would the State be open to PMPM payments to support cash flow for smaller providers investing in VBC/APM capabilities? Applicants may propose PMPM payments for consideration by LDH. Proposals should include justification and operationalization details for such monthly payments. 12. Can funds be used to staff support for data integration, analysis, and reporting related to this RHTP initiative? Yes, this would qualify as a form of technical assistance for infrastructure / capacity building under Lane 2. 13. Is provisioning devices and connectivity for members lacking reliable mobile access an allowable cost, given the social-need and telehealth exclusions? No. Provisioning devices and connectivity for members is not an allowable cost under this funding opportunity, consistent with the social need and telehealth exclusions. Applicants seeking to fund remote patient monitoring or telehealth-related capabilities, including member-facing devices and connectivity, are encouraged to review the forthcoming NOFOs dedicated to those areas. 14. Does LDH require community health worker (CHW) certification, or is a trained, non- certified CHW workforce acceptable? Applicants whose CHWs meet the qualification criteria in the Louisiana Medicaid MCO Manual will score more favorably (https://ldh.la.gov/assets/medicaid/MCPP/MCO_Manual_CHW_2022-06-30.pdf). The manual defines a qualified CHW as someone who has completed a state-recognized training curriculum approved by the Louisiana Community Health Worker Workforce Coalition, or has a minimum of 3,000 hours of documented work experience as a CHW. A trained, non-certified CHW workforce that does not yet meet these criteria will be considered if sufficient justification is provided, including a description of the training

Rural Medicaid APM Program Answers to Submitted Questions , 2026 curriculum, supervision structure, and a plan to reach the qualification standard. Aligning with the Medicaid qualification criteria also positions services for sustainability, since Louisiana Medicaid MCOs cover CHW services only when rendered by qualified CHWs meeting these criteria. Project Specific Questions 1. Our clinic already provides care coordination, chronic disease management, telehealth, and hospital follow - up. Is the intent to strengthen/expand existing workflows in preparation for VBC, or should proposed activities be entirely new services? Both. Applicants can use funds to strengthen and expand existing workflows in preparation for VBC and to add ne w, unreimbursed activities. If an applicant is in Lane 2 (paid for results), the expectation is that infrastructure / capacity building funds are used to scale / tailor the existing VBC model to rural providers. 2. Does the LDH VBC model follow HCP - LAN, and what is the target roadmap in terms of percentage of Medicaid members at various LAN levels at various points in time? While the LDH target care model is not expressly tied to the HCP-LAN framework, Lane 2 is intended for applicants that are ready to propose projects for upside-only shared savings (HCP-LAN Category 3A) or two-sided risk (HCP-LAN Category 3B) models. Applicants in Lane 1 are expected to be building the infrastructure and capabilities necessary to participate in these models and may also request performance payments for quality improvements (HCP-LAN Category 2). LDH recognizes that rural providers may have significantly different capabilities to successfully implement VBC models to impact TCOC and quality today. As a result, this NOFO does not establish a target roadmap for percentage of Medicaid members in various LAN levels over time. 3. Is the State willing to mandate a minimum data set that MCOs must share within a specified timeframe with providers entering various levels of risk sharing? The state is currently exploring options for shared data and analytics solutions for future grant years. This NOFO does not create any new obligations on MCOs to share data with providers. 4. If an MCO already pays a health center for quality/HEDIS/gap closure, and the lead applicant would also pay the health center for quality, is that duplicative? Applicants must describe how RHTP funds are not duplicative with existing sources of funding. RHTP cannot pay again for the same activity, measure, or population/period those programs already cover.

Rural Medicaid APM Program Answers to Submitted Questions , 2026 In this instance, applicant would need to describe how quality payments differ from those awarded by MCOs (e.g., differences in measures, populations, and/or time period) AND how any differences solve a clear problem that existing quality payments do not. 5. Only ~50% of the Medicaid population our providers actively treat is properly attributed by the MCOs. How will discrepancies between MCO and provider attribution be resolved to accurately reflect cost of care and population definition? This funding opportunity is independent of any alternative payment models provides may currently be participating in through a managed care organization (MCO). Applicants in Lane 2 should propose an attribution methodology that they believe accurately reflects the patients for whom they can manage quality and cost of care (it may mirror those from current arrangements the provider is in). Proposed attribution methodologies are subject to LDH review. LDH will work with potential Lane 2 awardees to refine and align on an appropriate attribution methodology prior to final award. 6. Given the absence of a single statewide health information exchange, will LDH facilitate access to managed care claims, eligibility, and admission-discharge-transfer (ADT) feeds for awardees, and on what timeline? The state is currently exploring options for shared data and analytics solutions for future grant years. Such access is not guaranteed as part of this NOFO. 7. The NOFO says the State may provide state-level data. What may be provided and within what timeframe? Specifically: (a) average premium paid to MCOs and TCOC by rate cell to set a benchmark; (b) detailed claims data (identified or de-identified) for population health/utilization analysis; and (c) data on quality measures and open care gaps? LDH will be able to provide applicants with the following data at the parish level, annually for SFY 2023-2025. Applicants may use these as directional inputs to describe how their projects will improve performance relative to regional baselines. LDH may work with potential awardees to evaluate availability of additional data prior to final award but cannot guarantee such availability. Total Medicaid members Total expenditures (PMPY) ED visits / 1,000 (including potentially avoidable visits) IP admits / 1,000 (including 14-day and 30-day readmissions) Prevalence and cost (PMPY) of the following conditions: cardiovascular, psychiatric, skeletal, central nervous system, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, diabetes, skin, renal, substance abuse, cancer, developmental disability, genital, metabolic, eyes, cerebrovascular, infectious disease, hematological, obesity

Rural Medicaid APM Program Answers to Submitted Questions , 2026 8. Lane 2 requires the provider receive 70% of shared savings. Our existing VBC/APM contracts with MCOs vary (some 50/50) with different cohorts, benchmarks, quality measures, and savings splits. Would we be required to amend those MCO agreements to comply with the 70% requirement? The 70% requirement applies only to any shared savings performance payments through this program. It does not impact any current agreements between payers and providers. 9. What is the MCO's role as an eligible partner? The applicant is responsible for defining the role of any potential partners. Areas in which MCOs could offer support include in data and analytics, member engagement, and technical assistance in implementing LDH's target care model. 10. Is becoming a managed-care-organization network provider required for award, or only for the Year 2 shared-savings transition? No, providers do not need to be contracted with a managed care organization to receive funding. This NOFO is focused on opportunities to expand the number of rural Medicaid patients that are included in value-based care arrangements. As a result, applicants should describe factors such as the size of their Medicaid patient population and how this program will impact how care is delivered to that population. Eligible Organizations/Programs 1. If we want our CIN to participate but our hospital already participates in LQN and MCIP, will our current payments from those programs be at risk, or is this initiative supplemental to them? Applicants must describe how RHTP funds are not duplicative with existing s ources of funding. RHTP cannot pay again for the same activity, measure, or population/period those programs already cover. 2. Can LDH confirm a technology or VBC - enablement vendor serving as a partner on multiple applications will not negatively affect eval uation of any individual application? Yes - non - provider partners (including technology and VBC - enablement vendors) can be part of multiple applicant teams. Each application is scored on its own merits. 3. Can a statewide, virtual-first provider group qualify as an eligible lead applicant under the independent primary care provider group category and serve rural members across multiple parishes rather than from a fixed site? Also, our Louisiana Medicaid enrollment is in process - must enrollment be complete at the application deadline, or is completion before the Notice of Intent to Contract acceptable?

keyDates.label: Funding is intended to help fill the gap and enable emergent and non-emergent healthcare access. *Applications are due by 11:59 p.m. CT on , 2026. *
keyDates.location: Many of Oklahoma’s rural communities are limited in their ability to acquire lasting assets that would demonstrably improve healthcare access, outcomes, and whole-person health. During stakeholder engagement used to develop Oklahoma’s RHTP application, many communities reported hours-long turnarounds when ambulances had to take longer trips, aging vehicles without the funds to replace them, and struggles activating Community Paramedicine programs without diverting existing EMS vehicles. OSDH anticipates *allocating** up to 20 grants, with individual awards of up to $350,000,* to eligible entities to purchase Community Paramedicine-specific vehicles or ambulances to serve the needs of rural Oklahoma and facilitate deployment of Community Paramedics. Applicants must currently provide mobile emergency medicine services, mobile integrated healthcare, community paramedicine, or related services in a rural Oklahoma community. *View the Emergency Medical Service and Community Paramedicine Vehicles Application* [ https://oklahoma.gov/health/rhtp/rhtp-funding.html ] ________________________________________________________________________ Other Open RHTP Funding Opportunities

keyDates.location: This program seeks to support rural maternal and child health by expanding access to doula care, focused on four distinct components: * *Expand training opportunities to prospective doulas* who would serve rural communities in Oklahoma across pre-conception, pre-natal, birthing, and post-natal periods, using an approved curriculum and ensuring that trainees are credentialed, enrolled, and trained on Medicaid claims processes * *Provide awareness-building and education for expecting parents* to better understand doula care, the support it provides, and the opportunities to have care covered via insurance * *Build stronger partnerships between other maternal health providers (e.g., OB/GYN) and doula providers*, including education about the role of doulas, resources to clarify referral processes, etc. * *Facilitate peer community and support for doulas across Oklahoma* to compare learnings and best practices (e.g., care strategies, support with billing), receive support from peers, and potentially provide shared services for independent doulas (e.g., billing co-op or shared resources for managing claims) *View the Expanding Care: Doulas Program Funding Application * [ https://oklahoma.gov/health/rhtp/rhtp-funding.html ] ________________________________________________________________________ *Visit the Oklahoma RHTP Funding Webpage to Learn More* [ https://oklahoma.gov/health/rhtp/rhtp-funding.html ] ________________________________________________________________________ *Please do not reply to this email. keyDates.location: BACKGROUND Kansas is a predominantly rural state comprised of over 100 community hospitals, including Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs), Rural Emergency Hospitals (REHs), and Prospective Payment System Hospitals (PPS). Providers across Kansas face duplicative credentialing processes, inconsistent requirements across payers, and prolonged onboarding timelines that delay access to care and revenue realization. To address these challenges, HEALTHWORKS, KHA Foundation Inc. (Healthworks) an established 501(c)(3) not-for-profit organization, is seeking proposals to develop a statewide Centralized Credentialing Verification Pilot Program (CCV) operating under a hosted model. The CCV will centralize credentialing intake and verification of healthcare providers while preserving payer credentialing authority and hospital privileging decisions. This project is supported with funding from the Rural Hospital Transformation Program (RHTP). Procurement will be conducted in accordance with applicable federal procurement requirements, including 2 CFR Part 200 and Federal Acquisition Regulations (FAR), as applicable. INTRODUCTION HEALTHWORKS invites qualified, accredited organizations to submit proposals to design, implement, and operate Centralized Verification Organization (CVO) services in support of the Kansas CCV. The selected CVO will serve as the primary source verification partner, performing credential verification of healthcare providers and securely sharing validated credentialing data with participating payers and other authorized entities. PROJECT LOCATION All services may be performed virtually, with statewide accessibility required. PROJECT OBJECTIVES The primary objectives of this pilot project are to: • Centralize and standardize provider credentials verification • Reduce duplicative credentials verification work across payers • Improve credentialing timeliness and data quality • Support payer delegation and National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) compliance • Facilitate discussions around standardization and provide guidance on policy and procedures related to the CCV Pilot • Enable secure, role-based sharing of verified credentialing data 2

data.title: RI - 2030 - RHTP Preparing for a Historic Opportunity to Strengthen Rural Healthcare Access and Sustainability

keyDates.label: State of Rhode Island Rural Health Transformation Program Preparing for a Historic Opportunity to Strengthen Rural Healthcare Access and Sustainability Overview On , 2025, H.R. 1 was signed into law , establishing the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) to improve rural healthcare across all fifty states. 1 The program provides federal funding from federal fiscal year (FFY) 2026–FFY 2030 to improve access, quality, and sustainability of rural healthcare. The program is administered at the federal level by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). 2 In Rhode Island, the application process for the RHTP is being led by an interagency team, including the Rhode Island Department of Health (RIDOH) and the Executive Office of Health and Human Services (EOHHS), working in collaboration with other state partners to coordinate Rhode Island’s response and guide statewide health system transformation. As part of the application, the State of Rhode Island will develop a Rural Health Transformation Plan to secure funding and guide investments that improve care delivery in rural communities. With RHTP funding, Rhode Island has the opportunity to strengthen local health systems, rethink how rural healthcare is delivered, modernize infrastructure, recruit, train, and retain our healthcare workforce, and build systems that remain viable long after federal funds expire. These funds are fully federally funded, and states are not required to provide matching dollars to access RHTP resources. View the Notice of Funding Opportunity from CMS. What We Know Today • Total Funding: $50 billion nationally over five years (~$10 billion annually). • Base Allocation: If all states apply, Rhode Island could receive ~$100 million per year for five years. • Discretionary Funds: Additional funds may be awarded based on rurality and other factors. • Administration: No state match required. No more than 10% of funds may be used for state administrative expenses. Funds must be used by the end of the fiscal year following the year in which they were allotted. • Timeline: o CMS released NOFO : September 15, 2025 o Application due: November 5, 2025 o Awards announced: December 31, 2025 o Program begins: Quarter 1 of 2026 What the State Must Do H.R. 1 requires states to submit a Rural Health Transformation Plan as part of the application. The plan must describe how the state will: 1. Improve access to hospitals and other providers for rural residents; 2. Improve healthcare outcomes of rural residents; 3. Prioritize use of new and emerging technologies that emphasize prevention and chronic disease management; 1 P.L. 119-21 Section 71401 Reg Text 2 CMS – Rural Health Transformation Program
keyDates.location: 4. Initiate, foster, and strengthen local and regional strategic partnerships between rural hospitals and other providers to promote quality improvement, increase financial stability, maximize economies of scale, and share best practices; 5. Recruit and retain clinicians; 6. Prioritize data- and technology-driven solutions that help rural providers furnish healthcare services as close to the patient’s home as possible; 7. Outline strategies to manage long-term financial solvency and operating models of rural hospitals; and 8. Identify specific causes driving standalone rural hospitals to close, convert, or reduce service lines. Allowable Activities (States must pursue at least three) 1. Promoting evidence-based, measurable interventions to improve prevention and chronic disease management. 2. Providing payments to healthcare providers for the provision of healthcare items or services, as specified by the Administrator. 3. Promoting consumer-facing, technology-driven solutions for the prevention and management of chronic diseases. 4. Providing training and technical assistance for the development and adoption of technology-enabled solutions that improve care delivery in rural hospitals, including remote monitoring, robotics, artificial intelligence, and other advanced technologies. 5. Recruiting and retaining clinical workforce talent to rural areas, with commitments to serve rural communities for a minimum of 5 years. 6. Providing technical assistance, software, and hardware for significant information technology advances designed to improve efficiency, enhance cybersecurity capability development, and improve patient health outcomes. 7. Assisting rural communities to right size their healthcare delivery systems by identifying needed preventative, ambulatory, pre-hospital, emergency, acute inpatient care, outpatient care, and post-acute care service lines. 8. Supporting access to opioid use disorder treatment services (as defined in section 1861(jjj)(1)), other substance use disorder treatment services, and mental health services. 9. Developing projects that support innovative models of care that include value-based care arrangements and alternative payment models, as appropriate. 10. Additional uses designed to promote sustainable access to high quality rural healthcare services, as determined by the Administrator. Why This Matters • Rhode Island’s rural communities face unique challenges, including limited access to care and workforce shortages. • This one-time federal investment offers a rare opportunity to build sustainable systems and expand access to care close to home. • Success depends on collaboration across providers, community organizations, payers, and residents. Next Steps and Stakeholder Engagement The Rhode Island Department of Health will host community listening sessions and will launch a Community Feedback Request process to collect input on priorities, needs, and innovative ideas from community partners statewide. Your insights will inform Rhode Island’s Rural Health Transformation Plan and ensure investments align with community needs. Contact For questions or to submit feedback, visit health.ri.gov/healthcare/rural-health-transformation-program or contact the Rural Health Transformation Program Team at RIDOH.OPCRH@health.ri.gov .

data.title: GA - 2026 - Rural Healthcare Facility Resilience Program Project Overview
data.highlights:
Georgia is launching a multi-year statewide initiative to assess and improve the resilience of 267 rural hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, and inpatient hospice facilities. The program focuses on enhancing infrastructure so facilities can safely shelter-in-place and serve as regional receiving centers during disasters. Assessment results will directly inform Georgia’s disaster response plans and support facility applications for infrastructure grants.

Eligible applicants include rural retail pharmacies and rural critical access hospital pharmacies serving Medicaid members.

keyDates.label: SECTION 1 -- GENERAL AND ADMINISTRATIVE ISSUES 1.01 Purpose The purpose of this Request for Proposal (RFP) # PHTHOET27002 is to solicit applications that will enable the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services (referred to as Agency) to select the most qualified applicants to implement the High-Risk OB and Neonatal Transport Initiative. This initiative will strengthen Iowa’s emergency maternal and neonatal care system by funding equipment purchases, non-reimbursable clinical services, workforce initiatives, continuing education and training. This procurement is supported by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) as part of a financial assistance award totaling approximately $209,040,063.71 over a five-year period with 100 percent funded by CMS/HHS. The contents are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily represent the official view of, nor an endorsement, by CMS/HHS, or the U.S. Government. Iowa’s year two award for this program is anticipated by , 2026 and budget amounts could change at that time. All activities presented within this RFP, including access to funds, are subject to CMS approval of the Agency’s year 2 budget. This work implements a portion of the EMS Community Care Mobile Initiative of the Iowa Healthy Hometowns Project, funded through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ Rural Health Transformation Program, opportunity #: CMS-RHT-26-001. 1.02 Contract Term The anticipated total Contract Term is from October 31, 2026, to September 30, 2031. Continuation of the Contract is at the Agency’s sole discretion and subject to: review of the Contractor and Subcontractor’s performance, Contractor’s and Subcontractor’s compliance with the special and general terms and contingent terms of the contract, availability of funds, program modifications, or any other grounds determined by the Agency to be in the Agency's best interests. The contract term, including all possible extensions provided by the Agency shall not exceed a six-year period. The issuance of this RFP in no way constitutes a commitment by the Agency to award a contract. 1.03 Eligibility Requirements Applicants must meet each of the following eligibility requirements for consideration. Eligible Applicants Public, private, nonprofit, academic institutions or governmental entities that provide Emergency Medical Services Care are eligible to submit an application in accordance with this RFP. Eligibility Requirements Eligible Applicants must currently be an Iowa Authorized EMS Transport Service. 4
keyDates.location: Eligible Applicants must serve as least one county with some parts or all parts of the county eligible for Rural Health Grants as described by the “Rural Health Grants Eligibility Analyzer ( Rural Health Grants Eligibility Analyzer )”. Electronic Communication Requirements Applicant is required to maintain and provide to the Agency, upon application, a current and valid email account for electronic communications with the Agency. Official email communication from the Agency regarding this application will be issued from grants@iowagrants.gov . Applicants are required to assure these communications are received and responded to accordingly. 1.04 Service Delivery Area The Agency aims to support High-Risk OB and Neonatal transport services in Rural Iowa. Applicants may be located in any county in Iowa, but must serve at least one county where some parts or all parts of the county are eligible for Rural Health Grants as defined by HRSA Rural Health Grants Eligibility Analyzer . Priority points will be awarded for serving a larger number of Rural counties. Priority points will also be awarded to Iowa ‑ authorized EMS Service Programs that attest to a commitment to providing interfacility transport services without preference for, or limitation to, facilities affiliated with a singular organization. To receive priority points, Applicants must upload a signed letter that commit to conducting transports among all eligible sending and receiving facilities throughout Iowa, regardless of health system ownership or management. 1.05 Available Funds The source of funding is federal funding from the Rural Health Transformation Program, authorized under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act . For the first contract year, the Agency anticipates awarding a total amount of approximately $6,000,000 for approximately three (3) awards. These funds will be for the time period of 10/31/2026 through 10/30/2027. The Agency anticipates approximately $20,127,987 total funds available for High-Risk OB and Neonatal Transport Initiatives for the entire contract term. Applicants will have the opportunity to apply for an approximate total four-year contract award of $6,709,329. The Agency reserves the right to award a different dollar amount to implement the High-Risk OB and Neonatal Transport Initiative for maximum coverage of Rural Iowa as determined solely by the Agency. The Agency anticipates adding funding each year via Contract Amendment throughout the term of the contract. (Refer to Section 2, Budget). Actual total awards and individual contract funding levels may vary from those listed or funding may be withdrawn completely, depending on availability of funding or any other grounds determined by the Agency to be in the Agency’s best interests. 5

keyDates.label: SECTION 2 – BACKGROUND AND SCOPE OF WORK 2.01 Background Iowa’s rural communities face persistent and intensifying public health challenges, including limited access to care, workforce shortages, and disparities in health outcomes. In response, the Agency developed the Healthy Hometowns initiative 1 as the state’s submission to the federal Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP), authorized under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 2 This initiative is designed to transform the delivery of healthcare in rural Iowa by building a high- quality, sustainable system of care that improves health, well-being, and quality of life for rural residents. Through the Iowa HHS Strategic Plan and Strategic Plan in Action 3 , the Agency has committed to elevate organizational health, advance operational excellence, and help Iowa thrive. The Iowa Rural Health Transformation Plan, Healthy Hometowns, is in direct alignment with those goals by promoting access to health and human services resources and helping individuals, families, children, and communities thrive. Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds set the foundation for Healthy Hometowns via House File 972 of the 91st Iowa General Assembly. This legislation, enacted , 2025, establishes a multi-prong strategy for improving rural health care access and health outcomes for rural Iowans. This plan revolves around the concept that Iowa describes as Health Hubs, often referred to as Hub and Spoke models of care. The vision for Healthy Hometowns is to implement a robust Hub and Spoke framework that supports long-term, sustainable and high-quality health care for Iowans living in rural areas. Healthy Hometowns has three primary goals: 1. Iowans will be able to get health care within their rural communities at the most appropriate locations for type and level of care thanks to support from newly developed partnerships, more rural primary care physicians and specialists, and upgraded equipment. 2. Iowans living in rural areas will have improved health outcomes with similar rates of morbidity and premature mortality to those living in Iowa’s more populous areas. 3. Iowa will invest in the development and utilization of innovative technology and data infrastructures to support sustainable care options close to home, seamless care partnerships, and data sharing throughout the state. The primary goal of this procurement is to equip EMS services with the tools, training, and clinical support needed to safely transport pregnant patients experiencing complications and newborns requiring advanced care in rural Iowa. This includes telehealth ‑ enabled capability, advanced maternal and neonatal monitoring, and coordinated pathways connecting rural “spoke” facilities to specialized perinatal “hub” facilities. The project aligns with the Healthy Hometowns goals of: • Improving rural access to emergency and specialty care; • Strengthening the rural EMS workforce; 1 https://hhs.iowa.gov/initiatives/rural-health-transformation-rht 2 https://www.cms.gov/priorities/rural-health-transformation-rht-program/overview 3 https://hhs.iowa.gov/about/strategic-plan 18
keyDates.location: • Integrating telehealth and the Iowa Health Information Exchange (HIE) into prehospital care; and • Reducing adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes across rural Iowa. The Agency and/or CMS reserve the right to deny any portion of the submitted application. The submission of an application with a large number of unallowable costs, including construction costs, may be grounds for disqualification. 2.02 Definitions A. RFP General Definitions. When appearing as capitalized terms in this RFP, including attachments, the following quoted terms (and the plural thereof, when appropriate) have the meanings set forth in this section. “Agency” means the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services. “Business Day” means any day other than a Saturday, Sunday, or State holiday as specified by Iowa Code § 1C.2. “Equipment” means tangible personal property (including information technology systems) having a useful life of more than one year and a per-unit acquisition cost that equals or exceeds the lesser of the capitalization level established by the recipient or subrecipient for financial statement purposes, or $10,000. “Request for Proposal” or “RFP” means a formal Request for Proposal that involves the state Agency soliciting bids to purchase services through a competitive process. “Performance Measures” means measures that assess the Deliverables or activity under this Contract. Performance measures include, but are not limited to quality, input, output, efficiency, and outcome measures. B. Definitions Specific to this RFP. When appearing as capitalized terms in this RFP, including attachments, the following quoted terms (and the plural thereof, when appropriate) have the meanings set forth in this section. “ALS for Obstetrics (ALSO)” means an interprofessional, multidisciplinary program that prepares healthcare providers to respond to emergencies during pregnancy, labor, and delivery. It emphasizes a team-based, standardized approach to improve maternal outcomes and patient safety, involving physicians, residents, nurse midwives, registered nurses, and other members of the maternity care team. "Ambulance” means any privately or publicly owned ground, fixed-wing or rotor-wing vehicle equipped with life-support systems and specifically designed to transport the sick or injured who require emergency medical care. “BEMTS Pilot Project” means the Bureau of Emergency Medical and Trauma Services (BEMTS)-approved pilot initiative designed to strengthen EMS maternal and neonatal 19
